title: The Wingdad
logline: Marvin Eriksen Sr. ditches Judy's twenty-stop itinerary to see the real New York, the Barney version, and Barney, expecting to babysit a sleepy Minnesota dad, discovers the greatest wingman of his life. While Marshall stews over losing his best friend to Barney, Lily, Ted and Robin cover for Marvin on Judy's itinerary, with Ted as Marvin in the photos and Robin as Marvin on the phone.
coldOpen: Kids, in the spring of 2013, Uncle Marshall's dad came to New York and asked your Uncle Barney to show him the real city. Barney figured he'd be babysitting. Instead, for the first and only time in his life, Barney got out-wingmanned. By a man in a fishing vest.

guests.name: Brick
guests.role: the bouncer at Velvet, the Meatpacking District club that has turned Barney away four hundred and thirteen times; keeps exact count, answers almost everything with one flat word, and melts completely for a Minnesota dad who asks about his mother

guests.name: Celeste Moreau
guests.role: an Atlantic City blackjack dealer who reads tells for a living, has turned Barney down three times (once in a fake mustache), and is immune to every play in the book except a proud dad

scenes.summary: Friday night. Marshall has been ready for his dad's visit since February and has planned Saturday's Eriksen Men's Night: fish fry and a Bigfoot marathon. Marvin arrives in a fishing vest with Judy's twenty-stop itinerary, which he has never once finished, and asks Barney for the real New York, the Barney version. Barney accepts, privately planning to have Marvin asleep by nine forty-five and use him as a sad-uncle prop on Celeste (imagined cutaway). Ted, Lily and Robin get drafted to cover Judy's itinerary. Walleye runner, take one: the size of a canoe. Marshall insists his dad will be home by ten. He was not.

beats.line: Marshall's dad was flying in for the weekend. Marshall had been ready since February.
He just texted from the cab. He spelled here with three e's. That's how excited he is, Lily.
Baby, sit down. You've checked the door eleven times.
He's my best friend. When I was eight, he drove four hours to a Bigfoot sighting because I asked.
It was a moose. He told me it was Bigfoot in a moose costume, so I wouldn't be sad.
So what's the big plan?
Saturday night. Eriksen Men's Night. All-you-can-eat fish fry in Bay Ridge, then a six-hour Bigfoot documentary marathon.
Your dad flew a thousand miles for a fish and a guy in a monkey suit.
He's not a guy in a suit, Barney. He's shy.
Son!
Marvin. Bold choice, the fishing vest.
Eleven pockets, son. Got a sandwich in one and a smaller sandwich in another.
And your mother sent this. Same as every visit.
Twenty stops. Every visit since 1982. I've never made it past breakfast.
beats.title: Marvin's Saturday in New York, by Judy
lines: 9:00 Statue of Liberty. Photo. NO saluting.
11:30 Saks, 4th floor. My scarf. On hold since 2009.
3:00 Empire State Building. Do NOT call it pretty tall.

beats.line: I'd take you out tonight, Dad, but I've got deposition prep till two. Tomorrow night, though, you're all mine.
Then tonight I want to see the real New York. The Barney version.
Marvin. The Barney version isn't a tour. It's a lifestyle. Most men don't survive it.
Son, I've survived forty Minnesota winters and one Lutheran church picnic that went real bad.
Every Sunday for nine years, my boy calls me with a new Barney story. I'd like to see one.
Dad, you'll hate it. It's loud, the drinks cost thirty dollars, and every girl is named Brooke.
Problem is Judy. She calls every two hours and wants a photo at every stop. Somebody's gotta be me tomorrow.
She scheduled the Empire State Building for three p.m., when the light hits the setbacks. Marvin, your wife is a genius.
Judy has had a scarf on hold at Saks since 2009? That's not shopping. That's a hostage situation.
I'm in.
Absolutely not.
Ugh. Fine. I'm Canadian. I'm legally unable to say no to a sad man in a vest.
Relax. Two beers at Velvet, one fish story, and he's asleep in a booth by nine forty-five.
And then what?
Then I've got a sleeping Minnesota dad. Celeste has turned me down twice. But a man caring for his elderly uncle?
Just resting my eyes, son.
Aww. Is that your dad?
My uncle. From a farm. I'm all he has left.
That's so sweet. Want to get out of here?
Let me just leave him a note.
You're going to use Marshall's dad as a prop.
An accessory, Ted. Like a pocket square. A huge, sleepy pocket square.
Say, did I ever tell you kids about the walleye?
Yes.
Tell it again, Dad!
Lake Mille Lacs, 1987. A walleye the size of a canoe.
That's the whole story?
That's the trailer, son.
Come on, son. Show me your New York.
Nine forty-five.
He's gonna hate it, right? He's from St. Cloud. He goes to bed when the walleye do.
Baby. He'll be home by ten.
He was not home by ten.

scenes.summary: One a.m. Marvin is in Barney's power seat, the limo is full of his new friends, and the walleye is now the size of a pontoon boat. Brick, who has turned Barney away 413 times, carried Marvin in because he asked about his mother. Marvin walked into Velvet and said 'Daddy's home', and it was true; he told Celeste 'Have you met my son? He's shy.' Ranjit reveals Marvin learned his wife's name in four minutes. Marshall calls and Marvin bumps Eriksen Men's Night for a rooftop pool party; Marshall said 'Sure, Dad' kind of high. Celeste tells Barney a man whose father brags about him that much might call back. 'He's not my father.' 'You touched your tie.'

beats.line: So I look down, son, and that walleye is the size of a pontoon boat.
Beautiful.
Four hours ago it was a canoe.
Walleye never stop growing, son. Neither do stories.
Brick. You have turned me away from Velvet four hundred and twelve times.
Thirteen. You tried the side door.
And tonight you carried him in. On your shoulders. Past the line.
He asked about my mom.
I've asked about your mom!
You asked if she was single.
Then he walked into the VIP room and said, Daddy's home.
And it was true! In nine years of saying it, it has never once been true!
Marshall says you say it. Figured it'd mean more coming from a dad.
And then he came to my table and said, hiya, have you met my son? He's shy.
I'm not shy! I came out of the womb doing finger guns!
That's why it worked.
Marvin, that's my move. You stole my move and made it better. I feel like a cover band.
Wait. Uncle Marshall's dad was cool?
Luke, for one weekend in 2013, Marvin Eriksen was the coolest man in Manhattan. Then he flew home and alphabetized his fishing lures.
Hello, Mister Barney! Mister Marvin knows my wife's name. Nine years, you never asked.
Of course I know your wife's name. It's Missus Ranjit.
It is Priya. She is knitting him a scarf.
Hiya, son! Is it one already? Gosh, time flies in a car with a bar in it.
Say, about tomorrow night. Celeste's got a friend with a swimming pool. On a roof, son. On a roof!
Sunday, then. Fish fry Sunday. I'll bring you a muffin. Love you, son.
How'd he take it?
Great. He said sure, Dad.
In a normal voice, or kind of high?
Kind of high.
I don't date men like you, Barney. But a man whose father brags about him like that? Maybe he calls back.
I don't call back. And he's not my father.
You touched your tie.
Marvin. Tell the walleye again.

scenes.summary: Saturday afternoon, item eleven: the Empire State Building. Ted is dressed as Marvin for Judy's photos and keeps pointing at cornices in them. Robin has been Marvin on Judy's calls since nine. Marshall, his Eriksen Men's Night bumped, has tagged along and is miserable: his dad is wearing sunglasses at night, and he doesn't swim, he floats, angrily. He can't lie to his mother when she calls, and learns Judy knew from the first photo: the itinerary is a thirty-one-year decoy so Marvin has something to escape, and she has loved talking to Robin's Marvin. Judy says Eriksen men don't wait to be invited, so Marshall heads off to be the most fun son in New York. Ted begs to finish the itinerary. Judy calls Robin to ask about their anniversary.

beats.line: By Saturday afternoon, we'd reached item eleven. And Marshall, whose Eriksen Men's Night had just been canceled, had come along.
Eighty-six floors of Art Deco, guys! Judy budgeted four minutes per floor for appreciating.
Ted. You're dressed as a Minnesotan grandfather.
Judy wants a photo of Marvin at every stop. From behind, I'm a perfect match.
From behind, you look like a coat rack that lost a bet.
And Judy wants to know why Marvin is pointing at a cornice in every single photo.
I can't help it if Marvin is passionate about cornices.
Hiya, Jude! You betcha. Sure is tall. Love you too, sugar beet.
She just asked if I'm wearing the good underpants.
Robin, how are you so good at him?
I grew up in Canada, Lily. Every man I ever met was Marvin. Including two of my aunts.
Barney sent another photo. It's my dad. In sunglasses. At night.
What's wrong with sunglasses at night?
Dad says only two kinds of people wear sunglasses at night. Movie stars, and Lutherans who've lost their way.
We were supposed to have fish fry. Instead he's at a rooftop pool with a bouncer named Brick.
My dad doesn't swim, Lily. He floats. Angrily.
Baby, he's allowed to have fun with your friends.
Not more fun! He's my best friend. Barney doesn't need my dad. Barney already has Ted!
Wait. I'm Barney's best friend?
Ted. Focus. You're Marvin.
Hi, Mom. Yep. Dad's right here.
He's not here! He's with Barney! Ted's been wearing a vest since nine a.m.!
Wait. You knew?
She knew at the Statue of Liberty. Dad salutes it every time. Ted just stood there.
I was appreciating the patina!
Nobody's finished her itinerary in thirty-one years. She writes it so Dad has something to escape. He has more fun that way.
It's a decoy. Judy's been running a play on her own husband for thirty-one years.
Barney would be so proud.
Then why does she keep calling?
She says Robin's Marvin is the best conversation she's had with Dad in years.
And she says if I want my dad, go get him. Eriksen men don't wait to be invited.
Tonight I'm going out with Dad and Barney. And I'm going to be the most fun son in New York.
You just said fun like it's a threat.
Because it is, Robin.
Guys. Nobody has finished this itinerary in thirty-one years. Item twelve is a carriage ride. With a blanket.
Fine. But I'm wearing the hostage.
Hiya, Jude.
She wants to know what I'm getting her for our anniversary.

scenes.summary: Saturday night pregame. Marvin is in a Barney suit from the emergency tailor; Barney is in Marvin's eleven-pocket vest. Marshall arrives suited up ('Daddy's home'), with his own Eriksen Playbook: the Lumberjack, ninety percent success, success meaning they take the granola bar. Marvin and Barney have a 'Brick!' fist bump. Barney tells the walleye, now the size of a Buick, and Marshall erupts: that's their fish, their weekend. Marvin and Barney finish the story: nine-year-old Marshall jumping in after it. Marshall fell in. Not the way Marvin tells it; he has told it to every bouncer in Manhattan, because Marshall's Sunday Barney stories make him snort. Barney admits the real thing: at Velvet's door, Marvin vouched for him as his son. 'I call everybody son. I only vouch for my boys.' Also, Brick let him in. Ted, Lily and Robin arrive having finished all twenty items; Robin has agreed, as Marvin, to an Alaskan cruise. Judy's sealed item twenty invites Barney home for Thanksgiving. Marvin leads everyone to the pool: he floats, angrily.

beats.line: Marvin, my tailor worked all night. He'd never done a Minnesotan. He had to tape two tape measures together.
And you look real sharp in my vest, son.
Eleven pockets, Marvin. Eleven. I've been carrying a wallet like an animal.
Gentlemen. Daddy's home.
Marshall. Your actual daddy is right there.
Hiya, son! You wore a suit? You said your wedding suit felt like a hug from a stranger.
Tonight I'm the wingman, Dad. I wrote my own playbook.
Ninety percent success rate.
beats.title: The Lumberjack
lines: Step 2: Tell her Barney is a great guy.
Step 3: Mention I'm married, so she isn't confused.
Step 4: Offer her a granola bar.

beats.line: Success at what?
She takes the granola bar.
Brick!
Brick!
Who's Brick?
Who's Brick, he says.
Go on, Barney. Tell him the walleye. You tell it better than me now.
Lake Mille Lacs, 1987. A walleye the size of a Buick.
It's a canoe! It's always been a canoe!
It was a canoe on Friday, Marshall. It's had a big weekend.
Dad, that's our fish! That's our story! He doesn't get our story!
This was supposed to be our weekend. You're my best friend. And you're doing the walleye with Barney.
Son. You never let me get to the end.
The line snaps. And a nine-year-old kid jumps into Mille Lacs in his church clothes and grabs that walleye with his bare hands.
Dad. I fell in. I tripped over the cooler.
Not the way I tell it.
He told that story to every bouncer in Manhattan. Brick knows your LSAT score.
Celeste knows about your Fiero. She's rooting for it.
Every Sunday you call me with what Barney did this week. You laugh so hard you snort.
I just wanted to see the New York that makes my boy snort.
Barney, I'm sorry. I thought you stole my dad.
I did. A little.
At Velvet, Brick said no. Like always.
Then your dad put a hand on my shoulder and said, this is my son, Barney. He's a good one.
I know he calls everyone son. But nobody's ever vouched for me at a door before.
I call everybody son, Barney. I only vouch for my boys.
Also, Brick let me in. Nine years, Marshall. Nine years.
We did it! All twenty items! The first complete Judy itinerary in history!
Ted, are you wearing my clothes?
Only from behind.
And I've been you on the phone since nine a.m. You're a great husband, Marvin. You just agreed to an Alaskan cruise.
She's been after that cruise since 1991!
Item twenty. Sealed. Only to be opened if somebody finishes. Robin, it says you make a wonderful Marvin.
And it says, Marvin, bring that Barney home for Thanksgiving. He looks like he needs a casserole.
Thanksgiving. In Minnesota. With a casserole.
Is there a bouncer?
There will be, son. We'll bring Brick.
Alright, kids. Rooftop pool. Everybody in.
Dad. You can't swim.
I float, son.
Angrily.
That Thanksgiving, Barney went to St. Cloud, and Marvin introduced him to every neighbor on the block as his son.
Brick came too. He's been to every Eriksen Thanksgiving since. He still won't let me into his club.
